title: How the pattern and level of employment change

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain how the pattern of employment shifts as an economy develops - between sectors, towards formal work, towards more women in the labour force and away from the public sector - and what moves the level of employment.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: The pattern and its drift
blocks.text: The pattern of employment is the split of the employed across sectors, occupations and regions, and between public and private, formal and informal work. As an economy develops, the share of workers in primary work - farming, fishing, mining - tends to fall and the share in tertiary work - shops, transport, tourism, offices - tends to rise, because richer households spend a smaller share of income on food and a larger share on services. Two further shifts run with development: changing social attitudes and wider schooling have raised the proportion of women in paid work, in Namibia as in Japan, and a turn towards a market economy tends to shrink the public-sector share as private firms take on more of the hiring, a movement Vietnam's state enterprises lived through.

blocks.heading: Formal work, women and the public sector
blocks.text: Three further shifts run alongside the move from primary to tertiary work. The first is towards the formal economy. Formal work is work in registered firms and public bodies, paid through payrolls, taxed, and covered by labour law and social security; informal work is unregistered - a street vendor in Oshakati, a mechanic fixing cars in a yard, a domestic worker paid in cash - with no written contract or protection. In Namibia a large share of workers are in informal work. As an economy develops, the formal share tends to rise: firms grow and register so that they can borrow from banks, win government contracts and sell to large buyers; more workers have the schooling formal employers ask for; and governments become better at enforcing registration and tax rules. South Korea's move from farms and small workshops into factory and office jobs shows the shift. The second is a greater proportion of women in the labour force. Changing social attitudes about whether women should work outside the home, more girls completing school and college, smaller families, laws against discrimination in hiring and pay, and the growth of service jobs have raised the share of women in paid work, in Namibia as in Japan. Where attitudes change slowly, or childcare is scarce, the share tends to rise more slowly. The third is a fall in the proportion employed in the public sector as a country moves towards a market economy. State-owned firms are sold, reorganised or closed, services once run by ministries are contracted out to private firms, and new private firms take on more of the hiring, so even where public jobs hold steady in number, they make up a smaller share of a growing total. Vietnam lived through this from the late 1980s, as private workshops and foreign-owned factories took on workers while state enterprises shed staff.

blocks.heading: Oshana's numbers
blocks.text: Read a worked example with invented figures. In 2016, of every 100 workers in Oshana region, 46 worked in primary occupations, 20 in secondary and 34 in tertiary; by 2026 the split is 28 primary, 20 secondary and 52 tertiary. The tertiary share rose by 18 workers in every 100 as tourist lodges outside Etosha and shops in Oshakati took people on. The level of employment moved as well: in a strong year of visitor spending the region's jobs grew by 4 000 workers, and in the drought-slow year that followed, 1 200 jobs went as spending weakened - the level riding the cycle while the pattern kept its long drift.

blocks.heading: What moves the level of employment
blocks.text: The level of employment is the number of people in work. It changes for two broad reasons. The first is the demand for workers: when total spending rises, firms need more workers and employment rises, and in a downturn it falls - the cycle seen in Oshana. Over the long run, growth in the economy's output tends to raise employment too, although new machines may let output grow with fewer extra workers. The second is the supply of workers: the labour force grows as the population of working age rises, as more women take paid work and as people migrate to find jobs. Because of this, employment and unemployment can rise together. Work invented figures through. In one year a region's labour force grows from 140 000 to 146 000 and the number employed rises from 120 000 to 124 000. Employment has risen by 124 000 - 120 000 = 4 000, but unemployment has risen too, from 140 000 - 120 000 = 20 000 to 146 000 - 124 000 = 22 000, because the labour force grew by 6 000, faster than the jobs. So a rise in the level of employment is good news for the people who found work, but on its own it does not show that unemployment has fallen.
